title: What not to put on the site for a manufacturer
metaTitle: What to cut from a manufacturer website
excerpt: Remove factory clichés, empty claims, and pages that only make the company look larger. Keep the object, the process, and a clear path to sales or a spec.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table, for a piece on editing a site down to what buyers need.
caption: A small group at one table. A shorter site can be this focused. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing to remove?
faqs.answer: Pictures and phrases that hide the product. Roofs, lobbies, spark showers, and claims like world class or full service. If a sentence can move to any supplier's site unchanged, cut it. Replace a true claim with the fact that makes it true.

faqs.question: Which pages are safe to delete?
faqs.answer: Pages with no job. Thin industry copies of one capability, unlabeled PDF libraries, and a blog that only recaps trade shows. Keep products, process, spec, proof, about, and contact. Redirect what you can, and drop the rest.

faqs.question: How do you keep the shorter site true?
faqs.answer: Give the stale facts an owner. Spec revision, the lead-time sentence, certificate scope, and the person named as reading drawings. Review them on the same rhythm as other controlled documents. The site is one of those documents.

markdown:
The manufacturer website mistakes that cost you the right buyers are usually acts of reassurance. A factory cliché with no product makes the team feel represented. It leaves a buyer who needs specs and confidence unsure what you make. Keep the object, keep how it is made, and keep a clear way to talk to sales or download a spec. A shorter site that tells the truth will outperform a long one that performs taste.

This is a cutting list. Walk the current site with it and remove what fails the buyer, even when it was expensive to produce. The space you gain is where the part, the process, and the next step can finally sit in the first screen.

## The factory cliché

Start with the pictures. An aerial of the roof. A lobby with a logo wall. Sparks with no joint in frame. A row of people in clean coats facing the camera, far from any object. Hard hats on a catwalk. These frames are easy to approve because they look like industry. They do not show the object, and they do not show how it is made.

Replace them, or delete them if the replacement does not exist yet. An empty slot with a plain sentence about the part is more honest than a cinematic miss. When you do have frames, use the object at a readable scale and the process step that carries the risk. One true sequence beats a montage of the grounds.

The same cliché shows up in language. State of the art. World class. Solutions provider. Partner of choice. Full service. If you deleted these phrases, the facts that remain are the site. If nothing remains, the phrases were the whole offer, and the page was never ready. Put back only claims you can attach to a machine, a material, a standard, a minimum, or a named role.

Video headers that play the cliché on a loop belong on this list too. They delay the part, they move under the headline, and they are miserable on a phone with the sound off. A still of the object starts faster and says more. If a process video exists and it shows the operation, use it on the service or the proof, with a still as the poster, and with the action still visible.

## Claims with no object attached

Superlatives without a scope. Badge walls without the certificate's coverage. "Trusted by leading brands" with no brands you are allowed to name and no job you are allowed to describe. A timeline of company feelings. A counter of parts shipped that nobody can define. They ask for confidence and then decline to show the work.

Numbers need a source inside the company. If you publish a lead time, a tolerance capability, or a years-in-process figure, someone must be willing to explain it to a visiting engineer. If they cannot, take the number down. An invented or orphaned statistic is worse than a quiet page. The buyer who checks will check.

Customer quotes need the same standard. A named person, a real role, a comment about a constraint you can discuss. Anonymous praise, "they went above and beyond," from a "global OEM" is filler. Leave it off. A single proof with a decision will do more work than a carousel of compliments.

Awards and rankings follow the same rule. If the award changed nothing a buyer can see, it does not belong in the first screen, and it may not belong at all. If it covers a specific process the buyer is buying, put it next to that process, with the year and the scope. A trophy case as the homepage is a tour of the team's pride. The buyer came for a part.

## Pages that exist to make the company look larger

Thin industry pages that repeat one capability under five market names. A blog that posts once a quarter about trade shows, with no answer a buyer could use. A resources library of unlabeled PDFs. A careers page linked from the header while the spec is buried. These pages add surface area. They dilute the menu and they create more places for a stale fact to hide.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks a site to have a clear purpose and to help a person who arrived with a real task. The purpose here is the object, the way it is made, and a path to sales or a spec. Pages that do not serve that purpose are the ones to cut.

Keep a page when it has a job. Products, the process, the spec, proof, about, contact. Add a note or an industry page only when the constraint is truly different and you can say how. Delete or combine pages that exist because a template offered the slot. A five-page site with a real spec is a stronger sales tool than a forty-page site of echoes.

Watch for duplicated offers. The homepage, the services page, and a "why us" page that all repeat the same adjectives. Choose one home for the argument and let the others point to it. Repetition feels like emphasis inside the company. Outside, it feels like you had nothing further to say.

Footer link farms, social feeds embedded in full, and a newsletter signup that pops up before the object is visible are the same mistake in smaller type. Put employment, privacy, and address in the footer. Let the social link be a link. Ask for an email after you have given them the spec, and accept that many buyers will never subscribe. They were never supposed to. They were supposed to judge the part.

## Motion, popups, and interruptions

A modal that asks them to subscribe, chat, or take a survey before they have seen the object is a self-inflicted bounce. Close it in your mind and then close it in the code. Chat widgets that cover the spec button on a phone belong on this list. If you want a conversation, use the contact path you wrote, with a window you keep. A pulsing bubble is not a window.

Autoplaying carousels hide the primary product behind a second slide the buyer may never see. They also move the thing someone was trying to read. Use a still. If you have several families, list them in text under the primary one. Text does not wander off while a person is deciding.

Stock music, cursor effects, and page transitions that delay the next view are taste performed at the buyer's expense. The site can be handsome. Type, spacing, a true photograph, and a calm grid are enough. Hanabi's own standard, clarity over complexity, is the right test. If the motion does not help someone see the part or reach the spec, it goes.

Cookie and consent banners should be real and brief, not a second homepage. Say what you use, let them decide, and return them to the object. A banner that pushes the headline down permanently, or that resets the page, is a defect. So is a banner you added because a plugin suggested it for a tracking stack you do not need. Fewer tools, fewer interruptions.

## Language that sends the wrong work

"We do it all" attracts the jobs you will later decline, and it repels the buyer who wanted a specialist. Publish the boundary. Materials, sizes, minimums, the processes you do not run. The fear is that a boundary shrinks the funnel. The reality is that a missing boundary fills the funnel with mismatches, and your best buyer cannot tell that you are for them.

Jargon from a brand workshop can do the same harm. If the plant says "the weld cell" and the site says "joining solutions," the buyer has to translate. Use the plant's nouns. The brand voice is the plain voice, used consistently. It is not a second dialect invented for the homepage and abandoned on the phone.

Hiding the price shape belongs on this list even when a public unit price does not. The mistake is a quote button with no model. Included, excluded, tooling, minimum, how a drawing becomes a number. If the buyer will ask, the site should answer the shape. Send them into sales with the shape already understood.

A contact form that demands a novel is a mistake you will feel as a quiet pipeline. Shorten it. Name the reply window you keep. Offer the spec on the same page. The detailed version of that path sits on its own page in this series. The cutting version is simple. If a field does not change the first reply, remove the field.

## Navigation and IA mistakes

A menu of departments. A header with no path to sales or specs. Labels that no buyer says. A search box on a tiny site. A resources item that opens a junk drawer. These are structural versions of the cliché. They organize the site around the company and hope the buyer will adapt.

Rebuild the bar around jobs. Object, process, spec, proof, action. Put the rest in the footer. Match each label to the heading on the destination. Click them on a phone. If the action disappears inside a closed menu, pull it back out. A buyer who has decided should not have to explore.

Orphan PDFs linked from old emails, outdated landing pages for a single trade show, and microsites with a different logo are part of the same cleanup. Pick one domain, one vocabulary, one action. Redirect what you can. Remove what you cannot defend. Confusion is a cost even when the analytics call it traffic.

## A shorter site you can keep true

After the cut, read what remains out loud. Homepage with the object, the making, and the action. Services with outcome, boundary, and next step. A price shape. An about page with people who own the work. A few proofs with decisions. A contact path with a short form. Specs that match the quotes. If a page does not serve that set, it needs a new job or a deletion.

Assign an owner for the facts that go stale. Spec revision, lead-time sentence, certificate scope, the person named as the one who reads drawings. Put a reminder in the same rhythm you use for calibration or document control. The site is a controlled document. Treat it like one.

Then look at the first screen on a phone, with the cliché gone. The object should be obvious. The next step should be obvious. That is the whole repair. Everything else is how you keep the next well-meaning addition from putting the roof shot back.

Book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min) if you want a studio to make the cut with you and rebuild what remains. Bring the current site and one spec you trust. The useful work is deciding what a buyer needs to see, and leaving the rest off.
